newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan warlord withholds recognition of Taleban.
newsitem.headline: Afghan warlord withholds recognition of Taleban.

text.p: General Abdul Rashid Dostum, a warlord controlling much of northern Afghanistan, withheld recognition on Sunday of the Taleban movement's new administration in Kabul.

"We do not recognise them (Taleban)," Mohammed Yussef, a spokesman for Dostum's Jumbish-i-Milli faction, told Reuters in an interview. "If they want to form a government, they must ask for our counsel."

The Taleban Islamic militia seized the Afghan capital on Friday virtually unopposed and set up an interim ruling council. It now controls most of the mountainous nation, torn apart by years of civil war.
Dostum's militia controls six northern provinces from its base in the bustling town of Mazar-i-Sharif 300 km (200 miles) northwest of Kabul.
It has thousands of well-armed men but has largely stayed out of the confrontation between ousted president Burhanuddin Rabbani's government and the Taleban.
Dostum himself, an ethnic Uzbek, has so far kept silent on events in Kabul. A Jumbish official said he would make a statement on Monday.
But the Taleban's capture of Kabul has placed the wily general, usually adept at playing off Afghanistan's warring factions against each other to his own advantage, in a precarious position.
Jumbish kept open the vital Salang highway, Rabbani's last supply route into Kabul not controlled by the Taleban, but there was little love lost between Dostum and Rabbani, an ethnic Tajik.
Rabbani, speaking from northeast Afghanistan, has urged Afghans to resist the Taleban, whom he described as puppets.
Relations between Dostum and the Taleban, a predominantly Pashtun and radically Islamic militia founded by students in 1994, are fraught with difficulties.
The Taleban says women should always appear fully veiled in public and will not be allowed to work.

Though most women walking the dusty streets in Mazar-I-Sharif wear long, pale veils that completely cover their faces, the territory controlled by Dostum is liberal compared to the strict Islamic Sharia law imposed by the Taleban.
"We're afraid of the Taleban coming," said a woman doctor in her 30s, her head only covered in a bright scarf. "If the Taleban come, I will not be able to work," she said.
